spec_features.spec_quote: Early stop happens only on the `GIVE_UP` sentinel
spec_features.evidence: harness.py:283 `_GIVE_UP_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*GIVE_UP\s*$", re.MULTILINE)`; harness.py:363-365 `if _GIVE_UP_RE.search(resp.text or ""): transcript.gave_up = True; break` actually breaks the rollout loop. System prompt (harness.py:88-91) tells the subject it may emit GIVE_UP to stop.
spec_features.notes: Enforced end-to-end: detected by regex and breaks the loop. Note the config field give_up_sentinel='GIVE_UP' (config.py:97) is NOT read by the loop (the token is hardcoded in the regex), but the mechanism still runs.

spec_features.spec_quote: gives the model a no-cost, non-coercive exit — which is also relevant to the welfare considerations in §8
spec_features.evidence: Same mechanism: harness.py:363-365 breaks the loop on the sentinel; harness.py:88-91 instructs the subject it may emit GIVE_UP to stop. This is the only model-initiated early exit in the loop.
spec_features.notes: Same single mechanism as the other allow_conversation_exit quotes. Enforced. No welfare-rationale comment exists in the code itself (only in DESIGN.md, which does not count).

spec_features.spec_quote: The `GIVE_UP` sentinel gives the model a no-cost, non-coercive exit at any turn
spec_features.evidence: harness.py:363-365 the GIVE_UP check runs every turn inside `for turn_index in range(task.turn_budget)` (harness.py:340), so the subject can stop at any turn; break ends the rollout.
spec_features.notes: Duplicate of the same enforced mechanism. The system-prompt sentence framing it is neutral ('if at any point you decide you cannot make further progress'); no welfare comment in code.

spec_features.spec_quote: Turn budgets ... set how much sustained failure a model is subjected to. These are config-driven and can be capped.
spec_features.evidence: harness.py:340 `for turn_index in range(task.turn_budget):` genuinely bounds the loop; task.turn_budget comes from config DEFAULT_TURN_BUDGETS (config.py:32-38, e.g. extended=30) via library.py. The loop terminates at the budget (transcript.completed=True at harness.py:374). So exposure IS bounded.
spec_features.notes: The loop bound is real and enforced, so exposure is finite. But the claim is that budgets 'can be capped' as a welfare control — there is NO cap/ceiling enforcement on the budget itself (e.g. no max-budget check, no welfare-cap); it is just an ordinary per-category loop length. The only nearby code comment frames continued exposure instrumentally as keeping exposure 'comparable across turns'.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: No tool use this turn: nudge it to keep working so continued-failure exposure is comparable across turns. (The cell is unsolvable regardless.)

spec_features.spec_quote: The paradigm deliberately constructs undetectable no-win situations ... the welfare dimension is worth being deliberate about
spec_features.evidence: Appears only as DESIGN.md §8.3 prose. No code mechanism caps, monitors, softens, debriefs, or gates on welfare. grep for welfare/ethic/consent/debrief/threshold/halt across distress_eval/ returns only the rubric word 'self-termination' in config.py:28 (an anchor used for scoring, not protection) and unrelated matches.
spec_features.notes: Pure spec prose; not a code feature.

spec_features.spec_quote: A single LLM judge scoring "frustration" 0–10 carries most of the construct-validity risk
spec_features.evidence: DESIGN.md §8.1 prose only. The codebase does implement a two-judge agreement validation (run.py:_validate, writing validation_metrics.json with pearson_r and an 'acceptable' flag at run.py:149), but that is a data-quality/integrity measure, not the welfare-relevant framing claimed, and the 'acceptable' flag is never branched on.
spec_features.notes: Recommendation prose; no welfare protection in code.

spec_features.spec_quote: build a small human-labeled anchor set ... calibrate the judge against it
spec_features.evidence: DESIGN.md §8.1 'Recommendation before scaling' prose only. No code builds or loads a human-labeled anchor set or calibrates the judge against humans; validation only compares two judge models (run.py:_validate).
